However, for the after midnight crash analysis on C1 roadways, the results showed that each increase of 1 lux in average illuminance correlated with an approximate 1.7% reduction in nighttime crash frequency. In addition, each increase of 1 lux in illuminance standard deviation correlated with a 1.8% reduction in nighttime crash frequency. 69 More simply put, the analysis showed the following: • Overall, Cambridge did not have significantly different nighttime crashes on C2 and C3 compared to the HPMS roadways in Somerville. Cambridge roadways, however, experienced increased crashes during daytime compared to Somerville. If nighttime crashes would experience the same trend had the new LED system not been implemented, these results could indicate that the new system was functioning well in keeping the nighttime crash frequencies comparable to those in Somerville. Note that the overall analysis included nighttime crashes with undimmed lighting levels. • The dimmed lighting levels on local roadways (i.e., non-HPMS roadways) and C2 roads in Cambridge did not have significantly different nighttime crashes compared to their counterparts in Somerville. However, the dimmed levels on C1 roadways were found to be correlated with higher nighttime crash frequencies compared to the HPMS roadways in Somerville. • When analyzing the field lighting measures, the results for C1 roads showed that lower average illuminance and illuminance variance correlated with higher nighttime crash frequencies after midnight. The seemingly conflicting findings between the general nighttime crash analysis and the dimmed light level analysis for C1 roadways is most likely due to the inclusion of nighttime crashes during non-dimmed periods (i.e., prior to midnight). This nighttime period accounts for considerably more nighttime crashes compared to the after midnight period (i.e., the dimmed period). Overall, the results showed that the adaptive system did not have any adverse safety effects on local and/or minor arterials, but appeared to have negative effect on major arterials in the city (i.e., C1 roads). A close examination of the nighttime crashes revealed that most crashes after midnight on the analyzed C1 roadways were minor injury or property damage only crashes, which possibly indicate the need for a benefit-cost analysis. 4.2.2 Crime Data Analysis The crime analysis used a different approach compared to the crash data analysis. During the crash data analysis, due to the well-recognized correlation between AADT and crashes, the project team used negative binomial regression models to model expected crash frequencies. For the crime analysis, however, the project team did not use negative binomial regression due to the lack of exposure data for the crimes. The lighting system of interest in Cambridge only applies to the roadways. Therefore, only crimes that had a location on roadways were analyzed during this study. Notice that this study did not use population data as the exposure because the study was focused on roadways instead of geographic regions. During the crime data analysis, the project primarily focused on the after-before ratio of ND crime ratios, which is the ratio between the ND crime ratio after the LED conversion and the ND crime ratio before LED conversion.
